en: *Caturyoginīsampuṭatantra* (The Tantra of the Union of the Four Yoginīs).

Toh. no. 376. Derge Kanjur, vol. GA, folios 44v.6–52v.5. Translated by Chings Yon tan 'bar [i.e., La chings Yon tan 'bar]. Manuscript = Tucci manuscript in folder 42 (the versos are available elsewhere, but have not been located for the time being).

Input by Péter-Dániel Szántó, Summer vacation 2012, Oxford. In the language of India: *Catuḥpīṭhayoginīsaṃpuṭatantra-nāma*. In the language of Tibet: *Rnal ’byor ma bzhi’i kha sbyor gyi rgyud ces bya ba* (The Tantra of the Union of the Four Yoginīs). *Namaḥ śrīvajravīrayoginībhyaḥ* (Homage to the glorious Vajra Heroes and Yoginīs).
[32] Homage to glorious Vajrapāṇi!
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *Caturyoginīsaṃpuṭa*.
Known as "The Four-Faced," it is concealed in all tantras.
Now, that which was to be correctly explained shall be taught: the union of the four yogas is analyzed as "the four faces," hidden within all the tantras.
Now, the faces and the union [of the deities] are clearly described;
they are renowned as being above and below, as well as on the left and the right.
It is explained as being below and above, and likewise on the left and the right. By means of the distinction between *āli* and *kāli*, it is established in the center of the navel;
it is renowned as the moon, the sun, the earth, and indeed the wind. (1.3)
By means of the distinction between vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), it resides within the center of the navel;
it is explained as the moon and the sun, and is endowed with the five elements: earth, wind, water, fire, and space.
Likewise, form, touch, and sound, together with the two eyes and the nose,
are perfectly endowed with space and the five elements.
Form, touch, and likewise sound, the two eyes, and the nostrils.
Situated both above and below within the body, the Vajra-holder is eternally established;
free from parts and portions,
he abides as the essence of the void.
Liberated from parts and non-parts, perfectly abiding in emptiness;
arisen from the end of *ya* with the letter *u* and a bindu, blazing and intensely radiant through the yoga of the hollowed-cup form. (1.6)

The final letter *ya* is complete and perfect; the letter *u*, together with the bindu, is joined and becomes manifest. Through the yoga of union, the Vajrin, intoxicated by *surā*, wanders with his consciousness fainting.
One sees the triple world in its entirety with the vajra-eye:
"Just as a person intoxicated by liquor, Upon sobering up, has his mind completely liberated, So too, the entire triple world Is seen with the vajra-eye. (1.7)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Indra, and likewise Kāmeśvara are seen by those who have attained the supreme siddhis of the seven kings, leaving nothing out and nothing remaining.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Indra, and likewise Kāmeśvara—
through the application of mastery over powers (*aiśvaryayoga*), through the prowess of Haṭhayoga,
and by means of the term "pledge" (*samaya*), these are spoken of as the primordial gods beginning with Brahmā. (1.9)
Having suppressed [the breath] by means of the power of the other, the Lord of Yogins is worshipped;
it is explained by the words of the *samaya* by the gods, Brahmā and the rest.
One should perform *prāṇāyāma*; by that, one possesses the restraint of the *samaya*.
In that regard, those renowned as the *sampuṭa* are established with four faces;
they should be known as the four yoginīs, endowed with the four yogas.
One should perform the complete vital breath and effort (*prāṇāyāma*); by that, this is the commitment (*samaya*) seal.
Regarding that, the aspects of the union (saṃpuṭa) shall be explained: it is established as having four faces;
it is called the "Assembly of the Four Yoginīs" and is perfectly endowed with the four unions.
Whatever sense faculty proceeds toward its respective object, that [proceeds] by way of its own intrinsic nature.
Through the enjoyment of all desires, one should maintain the samaya of all Buddhas.
Whatever arises from the path of each sense faculty, that very thing is its own nature;
through the enjoyment of all desires, it becomes the nature of all Buddhas.
How is the *bimba* produced? What is the nature of meditation therein?
How does the arising of mantras occur, and how is their perfection achieved? (1.12) How is the *bimba* brought to completion? What is the manner of cultivation in that regard?
How are the mantras to be generated? And how do they reach completion?
All that which arises from the tantras is merely a designation;
this mantra of the awakened mind (bodhicitta) is endowed with the five objects of desire. 1.13
All of these are merely conventional designations; from them, mantras and tantras truly arise.
Herein, the bodhicitta is praised; it is perfectly endowed with the five objects of desire.
It is the indicator (*lakṣaka*), the characterized (*lakṣya*), and that which is devoid of characteristics (*vilakṣita*).
The nature of the mantras has been clearly explained; now listen to the meditation on the deities.

Having extensively described the mantras, which are indicated by the characteristics of that which is indicated—though manifold, they do not indicate [anything else]—now hear the visualization of the deities.
At the upper gate there is a triad,
and at the pericarp is she whose form is wind; there, in the center, is always the void, resembling pure crystal.
In its center, it is eternally empty, like pure crystal;
emitting great enjoyments, the ninth is joined with the tenth.
The calculation is eightfold by means of the limbs; the seed is enclosed by nine gates. (1.16)

The great enjoyments emerge with certainty; it possesses nine and ten, and by means of its eight parts as limbs, it is the seed of the nine gates. Thus it is said: "Of the body, [the nature] consists of the goddesses who are the wisdom-ḍākinīs."

But the wisdom that issues forth from the upper portion is Vajradhṛk. From the body, the seed-syllable is uttered; by the nature of the Wisdom-Ḍākinī, it emerges in the upper direction together with Prajñā and Vajradhara.
That which is renowned as *cittavajra* is here called the upper lotus;
its location is declared to be the *bhaga* for the Vajrin of the Wisdom-Reality (*prajñātattva*).
(1.18) It is explained as the "Vajra of Mind"; here it is explained as the upper lotus.
In that regard, the location is explained as Bhaga; that very wisdom, together with the Vajra-holder, exists as the support and the supported, established within all the channels.
It flows in the form of semen for the sake of creation and dissolution. (1.19)
Abiding within all the channels by means of the dependent and the dependently arisen,
it performs the functions of expansion and withdrawal by having taken the form of the seminal essence (*śukra*).
Through the yoga of the generation stage, for the purpose of the process of meditative cultivation.

The cultivation of the deity has been explained according to the sequence of the *sāmnāya* yoga; that is, through half of the stages of meditation by means of the yoga of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*),
it is said that the deities are to be meditated upon by means of the yoga of the stages of oral instruction (*upadeśakrama*).
Through the yoga of the universe, their arising is that of the moon and sun;
through the yoga of the universe, the motionless image of the Buddha is liberated from both the supreme and the non-supreme. (1.21)
Through various yogas, these are explained as the moon and the sun;
furthermore, liberated from being other or not other, the form of the Buddha is immovable.
One should maintain concentration (*dhāraṇā*) there, wherever it may abide.
The Blessed One, the Wielder of the Vajra, is designated as day, and wisdom is designated as night. One should grasp that [reality] which abides therein in such a manner:
the Blessed One, the Wielder of the Vajra, is day, and wisdom is said to be night.
Beyond the sky, supremely peaceful, auspicious, pure, and free from ailment—
[therein dwell] all the Buddhas and others, the non-Buddhist teachers, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
(1.23) Having entered the expanse of space, supremely peaceful, Pure, virtuous, and delightful.
Buddhas and all others, including the non-Buddhists, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas—she herself is passion and dispassion; she is desire and liberation.
She herself desires women, and she herself conceives the embryo. (1.24)
That very [reality] is passion and freedom from passion; through desire, it becomes liberation itself.
That very [reality] is attached to women; that very [reality] takes up the womb.
It is death itself, it is situated in the body, and it is that which withers as it perceives.
That very [entity] becomes the gandharva; that very [entity] is established as the embryo.
That very [entity] dies and remains as a solid mass; that very [entity], being dried up, is what is seen.
That very [entity] has become elevated; that very [entity] abides as fragrance.
She alone experiences sufferings as well as the pleasures of touch.
And by that single [reality], which exists in the form of the drop of nectar (*amṛtabindu*),
suffering is known; through that very knowledge, one is pervaded by bliss itself, by that alone,
in the form of the drop of nectar.
He is handsome, possessed of beauty, foremost, manifold in form, and made of mind.

The glory of the manifestation of all forms, the bearer of every reflection; the supreme among those endowed with beautiful form, possessing various lovely forms, the splendor that illuminates all forms, the holder of all images without exception.
The knower of reality always [perceives] that which is sixteen, half of that, and half of that again;
the universe is eternally peaceful, the reflection endowed with the five voids. (1.28) Sixteen, half of that, and half of that; the knower of reality is always [present].
The form that is eternally peaceful and manifold is perfectly endowed with the five spaces;
they say that very [form] is the entry, illuminated like light for the world.
Having emerged from the tip of the nose, blazing with a garland of rays, it is said to have entered that very [tip]; like a lamp illuminating beings,
it issues forth from the tip of the nose as a mass of blazing light.
I shall explain all of this, characterized by the relationship between the substratum and that which is supported.

But he who, having understood that she is known through the ritual as "the Accomplished One," knows her as the extensive glory— 1.30— I have described all these for him in terms of the characteristics of the support and the supported; by knowing this, his prosperity will be fully accomplished.
I shall explain another collection of mantras, a secret yoga hidden in mystery:
having extracted the final group of eight [consonants], it is endowed with five seed-syllables. (1.31) Furthermore, I shall explain the collection of mantras; this secret application is concealed.
One should grasp the end of the eight groups; it is perfectly endowed with the five seed-syllables.
Then one should provide the syllable *bhrūṃ*, accompanied by the primordial breath.
The letter *a* is the foremost of all phonemes, the great bindu, which is beyond syllables. (1.32)
Therefore, one should bestow the syllable *bhu*, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*.
The letter *a* is the supreme of all letters; it is the great bindu (*mahābindu*), devoid of syllables.
It abides in the center of the space of space, arising from the mantra and tantra.
And as for the mantra, it arises from the form of the aspect of suchness;
just as space abides in the center of space, so too do the mantra and the tantra truly emerge.
Just as it is with that [space], so too is the mantra, appearing in the manner of suchness.
And the phoneme (varṇa) conjoined with its vowel measure (mātra) is proclaimed to be situated there in the middle.
The Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and whatever other hosts of deities there may be,
are renowned as being centered upon that which is perfectly endowed with even a mere syllable.
The assembly of the great elements and so forth, as well as the gods, asuras, and guhyakas—
therein they were born together in the center, possessing forms that are imperishable and beginningless. (1.35) All beings without exception, the gods, asuras, and guhyakas.
In its center, she is perfectly complete; by means of forms such as syllables and so forth, she is Rūpiṇī, Yoginī, Lāmā, and especially Khaṇḍarohā.

They are renowned as "Four-Faced" and are endowed with the four yogas. They are explained as "Four-Faced" due to the distinctions of the forms of Yogāmbara and Ḍombī, and they are perfectly possessed of the four yogas.
Endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and possessed of four petals;
there in the center, O Great Hero, he is adorned with eight arms.
With a navel and filaments, and perfectly endowed with four petals—
therein, in the center, is the Great Hero, adorned with eight arms.
The first [petal] is filled with flesh, and the second is likewise blood.
The first [skull] is filled with flesh; the second is filled with blood; the third and fourth are the body-mudrās, the *khaṭvāṅga* and the *ḍamaru*. 1.38.
It has the luster of shimmering, firmly established colors, as stainless as the autumn sky.
White, red, black, and green, they follow after the faces; likewise,
white light radiates forth like the stainless autumn sky—
white, red, and likewise black, with faces that are green and fierce.
The eight mudrās have been fully described, as well as the arms and weapons proclaimed [for the deities].
The first is the mudrā of melting; the second is the drawing-in of the heart. These eight mudrās are explained in brief; they are renowned as weapons held in the hands.
The first is the mudrā of entry; the second is the extraction of the heart.
The third is the mohanī mudrā, and the fourth is likewise the panī.
The third is the bewildering mudrā; the fourth is likewise the causing-to-fall. The fifth is the dancing mudrā; the sixth is declared to be the slaying mudrā. (1.41)
The seventh is the mudrā of the Devourer; the eighth is the Mistress who certainly takes [the offering] above. Yama, Bhīṣaṇī, Caṇḍikā, and Ghasmarī—

*Bhā* and *su-ma*, as well as *kāma* itself— these eight are Vārāhī herself. One should meditate on the Vajraḍākinī, who has a formidable and transformed form, who consumes blood and semen, and blazes with various flickering rays of light.
The wisdom that explains extensively arises therein as the center;
it illuminates an expanse of one hundred thousand *yojanas*.
It is without beginning or end for sentient beings, the great passion of Vajrasattva.
He becomes the possessor of the vajra-bindu, radiant like a half-moon;
his seat is a ruby lotus, and he is clearly manifest in the form of a king.
He is explained as "the state of kingship" itself, renowned for arising above.
Furthermore, they are to be arranged; they are described according to their classification by family.
In the east, one becomes Vajrasattva; in the south, Vairocana is proclaimed; in the west, Hayagrīva; and in the north, Padmanarteśvara.
In the center of the wheel is Heruka; the upper [face] is that of a horse-head.
It is taught that these are to be placed here. Through the differentiation of the families, there are five aspects;
they are to be meditated upon therein as being indestructible and unbreakable.

In its center is perfectly complete the Great Tantra known as the *Saṃpuṭa*, which is brought forth by the assembly of the four yoginīs, beginning with the Protector Vairocana; this concludes the first chapter.
Then that Vajravārāhī, adorned with anklets and necklaces, performs a dance within that maṇḍala; she bestows empowerment in order to firmly establish [the practitioner] in the samaya.
Thus does Vārāhī act toward the one who possesses the vajra.
"O Vajradhara, tell me: do you desire it thus? Do you eat excrement and urine, as well as blood, semen, and flesh? Are you always capable with women?
Do you kiss the lotus of the bhaga? Speak, O Vajradhara of Great Bliss!"
Then the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, smiled and said these words:
“O Goddess, why should I not take pleasure? I shall eat blood, semen, and so forth;
I shall always honor women and offer my kisses upon their lotus-like vaginas.”
Again, [the master] says, "Excellent! Excellent! Then the gatekeeper, likewise possessing the vajra, takes up a skull-cup and offers food to the one possessing the vajra;
he sits naked and peaceful, while the one possessing the vajra has his hair loosened.
He bestows the excellent empowerment. O Vajra-holder, you who cry out "Bhaga," from this moment forth, O Vajra, perform the noble conduct for the sake of sentient beings:
consume the great fragrance, the fragrant water, blood, semen, and flesh.
One should offer [the oblation] into the lotus of the bhaga; the nectars are to be accomplished.
Then, the male and female messengers of the Vajrayoga always confer empowerment.
HŪṂ HŪṂ HAḤ HA HA HA HA HRĪḤ HRĪḤ SVĀHĀ.
Then, immediately thereafter, Vajradākinī herself proclaimed a great sound: "That Vajra-holder is empowered!
He of manifold forms, the Great Fierce One, is perfectly seated upon a skull-throne."
They drink flesh and blood, joined within the secret maṇḍala;
some play musical instruments such as the *pataha* and *mukuṇḍa*;
some sing songs most excellently, while others hold up lutes.
Some dance for the wielder of the vajra; some ring the bell. Some produce the sound of the *phetkāra* [shrieking] in the ten directions. 2.12.
Some, O Vajradhara, perform the dance; some proclaim the sound of the bell.
Some utter loud cries, and the sound of "pheṃ" resounds in the ten directions;
some perform dances, while others sing within the maṇḍala.
Some scatter flowers for the consecrated Vajrin; some perform songs in the mandala; some distribute flowers. By these means, they consecrate the Holder of the Vajra.
Some will offer incense, and others likewise will offer fragrance.
Such is the worship for you, the miraculous manifestation of the secret wheel:
some offer excellent incense, others likewise with perfumes;
with such worship as this, one should perform it for the secret maṇḍala.
Then that goddess Vajriṇī uttered these words:
"The consecration has been correctly explained, as well as the maṇḍala of the Gaṇas. (2.15) Then that goddess Vajriṇī spoke these words.
Having properly explained the purity of the maṇḍala of the assembly and the empowerments, I shall now describe the supreme placement of the deities:
it is square on all sides, with four doors and eight cubits [in extent]. 2.16
I shall further explain another [subject]: the supreme laughter of the deities.
Eight cubits in every direction, square and with four gates—the mantra practitioner should wander twice that size and worship the playful display of the *ḍākinī*-net.
The mantra practitioner should worship the supreme maṇḍala, twice the size of that [previous one], where the assembly of ḍākinīs exults; wherever it pervades the expanse of space with its radiance,
that is the supreme maṇḍala.
Having drawn a wheel in the center, provided with a pericarp and filaments.
One should correctly draw a wheel in the center,
complete with a hub and filaments,
endowed with four petals, and perfectly white in color. 2.18.
There, in the center, one should place the Hero, stainless like pure crystal;
smiling, his first face gazes with eyes that are like the letter *lā*.
The first face is wide open; with the first eye he gazes intensely.
His brow is knit in a frown, blazing brightly, and terrifying with its formidable fangs.
The face turned to the south is wrathful, with a clearly manifest frown; its bared fangs are terrifying—these are the faces looking toward the south. The left [face] is marvelous.
On the back, however, there is a most terrible [form] situated at the mouth of the seven kings.
White, red, likewise black, and green are described [as the colors]. The back is greatly fearsome; the front and back are adorned with horse faces.
White and red are situated there, as well as the color green.
Having depicted him with eight arms, adorned with a garland of skulls.
Wearing a garland of severed heads, he is terrifying and fearsome;
his eight arms should also be drawn, adorned with a garland of skull-cups,
holding a glorious string of heads, and his tongue is rolled back in a display of dread.

Terrifying like a cremation ground at the time of the great dissolution, it resounds with loud laughter, great laughter, and the sound of howling cries. (2.23) It is like the fire of the great eon of destruction; it is as fearsome as a charnel ground.
Laughing boisterously and laughing loudly with a sound of "pheṃ," she is described as having two arms and one face, and is accompanied by four goddesses;
holding a khaṭvāṅga and a cup in her hands, she drinks blood and semen. 2.24
With one face and two arms, the four deities are to be described;
holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup in their hands, they drink blood and semen.
In the second wheel (*cakra*), a circular moon-maṇḍala is taught.
The great eight-syllable wheel blazes with red rays of light. [The second wheel is correctly explained: upon a circular lunar mandala, || 2.25 ||
The eight syllables of the Great Wheel blaze with red light rays;
they are known as Rūpiṇī, Dīpā, Śalmalīkā, Avivartinī, Ehikī, Vajriṇī, and the eighth. 2.26
Rūpiṇī, Cumbanī, Varottaravardhanī, Sāmali, Avaivartikā, Ehi-ki, and Vajriṇī are said to be the eight;
these eight goddesses are to be placed here, white in color and brilliantly radiant.
Holding a *khaṭvāṅga* in her hand and a skull-cup filled with blood—
these eight goddesses should be placed here, white in color and intensely radiant.
Holding a skull-cup filled with blood in her hand, she grasps the throat with her hand.
This is taught as the outer wheel, the supreme placement of the deities:
Sakhinī, Pukkasī, Māraṇī, Gaurī, and likewise Sphoṭanī.
The outer wheel is perfectly described, with the array of deities and their offerings:
Saṃkhinī and Pukkasī, Ghasmarī, Śvetā, Rākṣasī, Caṇḍālī, Śabarī, Tāraṇī, and likewise Bhṛkuṭī.
Trailokyavijayā, Ghasmarī, and likewise Caṇḍākṣī, Śavarī herself, Tārā, and similarly Bhṛkuṭī, Trailokyavijayā, Mahāmāyūrī, and likewise Ghasmarī.

Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, Brahmāṇī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī—these are proclaimed as the gatekeepers and are stationed at the four gates. (2.30) Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā, and likewise Brahmāṇī and Vaiṣṇavī, Are declared to be the gatekeepers and are assigned to the four gates. (2.30)
The correct explanation of the gatekeepers is as follows; they are to be applied at the four gates:
A great wheel of blue color, its radiance filled with garlands of flames; and the Great Goddess of white color, holding a conch and a khaṭvāṅga staff. (2.31)
The Great Wheel is blue in color, with the radiance of a mass of blazing garlands;
the Great Goddess is white in color, holding a *khavajra* and a mirror.
This is the King of Mandalas in the Samvara of the Four Yoginīs.

In the independent [tantras], there is a general mandala that becomes increasingly superior. This mandala is the king; it is the common [practice] within one's own tantra, the commitment of the four yoginīs, and the mandala of the Guru of Gurus.
The vow of the Great Churner is said to be his Guru.
This concludes the second chapter, titled "The Examination of the Mandala," from the *Yoginīcatuḥsaṃpuṭa*.

Next, furthermore, that which is to be explained is the *Sādhana* of the Great Samaya. The lamps of the elephant, horse, donkey, ox, female camel, and dog are fully revealed; the Great Lamp is thoroughly explained. Making the world joyful, it illuminates clearly. The five—crow, owl, hawk, water-fowl, and vulture—are explained as the "Great Incense"; they are offered as incense. By these, one will bring [beings] under control and roam throughout the three worlds. As long as the collection of applications is complete, it is the supreme performer of all *siddhis*. The Five Nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are described: they are the state of immortality, yet not a substantial entity. One should consume them without conceptualization, for the wise are devoid of intrinsic nature. Having extracted the mantras of the final section, endowed with the sixteenth part, one places the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) above, marked and adorned with the *bindu*. This is what is everywhere called "Fragrance. Below the heart-mandala, the twenty-seventh is provided; it is correctly joined to the crown. The letters, in the form of deities, are joined as twenty-six, adorned with the second vowel. The twenty-third is also taken and joined to the lower portion. It is endowed with the third vowel and joined with the fourth. In its center, it is correctly spoken; it is adorned by the letter Īśvara (I). The end of the sixteenth is correctly explained; it pervades above and below. In its center, it is correctly spoken: the letter of the Great Praise, the indestructible Vajrasattva. Like pure crystal, these substances are to be consumed. These yogas are supreme; they are most exalted above all yogas. I have explained them to you in brief; the foods are correctly described. Whatever is edible according to reason, having mixed things of equal taste, one should not distinguish between pure and impure. All suchnesses and all foods should be consumed. Through the excellent differentiation of the ten realities, one is liberated from subject and object. One should give the essence of generosity. Having perfected the yoga of the mind, one should abandon everything like grass. This is the ethical discipline of the Buddhas; through all suchness, there is fearlessness. One does not harm any living being. First, there is unsurpassed compassion, patience, and unimpeded ethical discipline. Obstructing the harm of others, the tent, the stake, and the net destroy the wicked Māras. Being without Māra, one is deathless. One's own mind should be bound; when one’s own mind is tamed, what need is there to mention the harm of Māra? With the fragrance of an equanimous mind, one should correctly draw a four-sided [mandala]. On the body, with aloeswood and sandalwood, the mind abides in equanimity. This is called the Wisdom of Equality. Mixing things that lack self-nature, whoever becomes a King of Yoga, whatever the male and female yoginis may consume, by that, throughout the entire earth, aging and illness are utterly destroyed.
The third ritual manual, named *Mayāpañcāmṛta*.
This is the third chapter, titled "The Five Nectars of the Great Samaya," from the *Yoginī-catuḥ-sampuṭa*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of the initial yoga;

for yoga is to be known as fourfold, accomplished through the four samayas. 4.1 Next, I shall correctly explain the sādhana of the initial yoga. Yoga is to be known as fourfold, accomplished through the four samayas. 4.1 Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of the initial yoga; for yoga is to be known as fourfold, accomplished through the four samayas. 4.1 Next, I shall correctly explain the sādhana of the initial yoga. Yoga is to be known as fourfold, accomplished through the four samayas. 4.1
One should know the four applications; the four pledges are to be accomplished.
The first is to be known as semen, and the second is likewise blood.
Vajra-water and feces are the practice of the four commitments. First is semen; second is likewise blood;
vajra-water and great fragrance are the observance of the four commitments.
Passion is explained as semen, and envy is indeed blood;
delusion is King Vairocana, and hatred shall become water. (4.3) Passion is explained as semen, and envy is indeed blood.
Delusion is King Vairocana, and hatred is together with the scent-water.
By means of the yoga of the four commitments, one who partakes of the four commitments shall become equal to Vajrasattva through the initial yoga in the final goal. 4.4
By means of the yoga of the four commitments, the practitioner who engages in the four commitments will first achieve the preliminary application and become equal to Vajrasattva.
One should accomplish the reality of the commitment (*samayatattva*) through the yoga of the descent of the *paṭa*.
One should utter the *śūnyatā-vajra* and visualize the *jñānasattva*.
By means of the yoga for inserting [the deity] into the painted image (*bris-sku*), one should accomplish that very reality of the commitment (*samaya*);
one should utter the *śūnyatā-vajra* and clearly contemplate the *jñānasattva*.
One should recite the mantra with intensity; one should utter the mantra beginning with *hūṃ*.
One should meditate with a state of being that brings about emanation and reabsorption. (4.6) In brief, the mantra is to be recited; the mantras beginning with *hūṃ* are to be uttered.
One should meditate through the meditation on the [inner] entity; it performs expansion and contraction.
But for the defeat of the four Māras, there is the binding with the horse-armor and so forth;

Then, furthermore, that which is to be explained is all the yogas of reality (*tattva*): generosity, ethical discipline, diligence, as well as meditative concentration, patience, wisdom, power, likewise skillful means, aspiration, and the perfect arising of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). The perfection of the ten [pāramitās] is taught as the four types of generosity within the bodhisattva vow; ethical discipline is the essence of the three [types]; meditative concentration is said to be of four types; diligence becomes fivefold; patience is to be known as tenfold; wisdom becomes sixfold; power is proclaimed to be tenfold; skillful means becomes fivefold; aspiration is to be known as twofold; and primordial wisdom abides in five ways. The four types of generosity—Dharma, fearlessness, material things, and loving-kindness—are the perfection of generosity. Abiding without ego-grasping and free from arrogance, dwelling in the non-duality of the two truths, what is called the threefold ethical discipline is taught as the perfection of ethical discipline. That by which the two yoginīs and the two external forms are taught is the perfection of meditative concentration. Great excrement, urine, as well as flesh, blood, and semen perfectly arise; these are the five types of diligence expressed by the term "pledge" (*samaya*). Harsh words, lies, and idle chatter...
